reconcile.connective: Defenders read 19:24 not as a rival origin but as a renewal of a proverb already coined in chapter 10, so only one saying with one source is in view.

discrepancy.connective: Julius Wellhausen, the founder of the source-critical analysis of Samuel, argued that the two prophesying scenes are independent parallel traditions, each supplying its own explanation of the saying — a doublet rather than a single proverb re-applied.

skeptic.name: Julius Wellhausen
skeptic.attribution: Julius Wellhausen (d. 1918), Der Text der Bücher Samuelis (1871)

excerpts.excerpt_text: This new occurrence in Saul's life occasioned a renewal of the proverb: "Is Saul also among the prophets?" The words "wherefore they say" do not imply that the proverb was first used at this time, but only that it received a new exemplification and basis in the new event in Saul's experience. The origin of it has been already mentioned in Sa1 10:12, and the meaning of it was there explained.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the doublet charge: explicitly denies that 19:24 originates the proverb, asserting one origin (10:12) and treating 19:24 as a renewal — the single strongest harmonization of this exact tension.

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament: The Books of Samuel (1861-75), on 1 Samuel 19:18-24
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: Keil treats this passage directly, arguing the proverb originated at 10:12 and was merely renewed at 19:24, against the doublet reading.
